title: Vicarious liability makes a master liable for the torts of a servant committed in the course of employment (Qui facit per alium & Respondeat Superior)

content.overview: Vicarious liability makes a master liable for the torts of a servant committed in the course of employment (Qui facit per alium & Respondeat Superior). Distinguished by control and integration tests. In India, sovereign immunity under Kasturi Lal has been superseded by constitutional tort compensation under Art 21 (Rudul Sah, Nilabati Behera).

content.study:
Topic at a glance
Vicarious liability is a legal doctrine under which one person is held legally liable for the tortious acts or omissions committed by another, despite being entirely blameless themselves. The most prominent application is the liability of a Master for the torts of their Servant committed in the course of employment. In public law, it governs the liability of the State (Sovereign) for the wrongful actions, custodial torture, and negligence of public officials under Article 300 and Article 21 of the Constitution of India.

Foundational maxims and juristic rationale
The doctrine is anchored upon two ancient Latin maxims:
1. Qui facit per alium facit per se: "He who does an act through another is deemed in law to do it himself." The principal who directs or employs an agent/servant is legally identified with the physical actor.
2. Respondeat Superior: "Let the superior answer." The master occupies a superior economic position and reaps the commercial benefits of the enterprise; therefore, the master must bear the burden of risks created by that enterprise.
Modern economic justification: The master possesses the "deeper pocket" and can distribute risk through commercial insurance and product pricing, ensuring that injured victims receive effective civil compensation rather than empty judgments against impecunious employees.

The three essential ingredients of Vicarious Liability
To fix vicarious liability on an employer, three conditions must be established:
1. A Recognized Relationship: There must be an established legal relationship between the defendant and the wrongdoer, typically:
   - Master and Servant (Employer and Employee)
   - Principal and Agent
   - Partners in a Partnership Firm
2. Commission of a Tort: The servant must have committed an actionable civil wrong (e.g. negligence, fraud, conversion, trespass) against the plaintiff.
3. In the Course of Employment: The tortious act must be performed by the servant while acting within the scope or course of their employment.

Distinguishing a Servant from an Independent Contractor
An employer is vicariously liable for the torts of a servant, but generally NOT liable for the torts of an independent contractor (unless the duty is non-delegable or the employer authorized the unlawful act).
The tests for distinguishing a servant from an independent contractor have evolved:
1. The Control Test: Historically, a servant is a person subject to the command of the master as to what work shall be done and the manner in which it shall be done (Performing Right Society v. Mitchell & Booker Ltd.).
2. The Integration / Organization Test: Formulated by Lord Denning in Stevenson, Jordan & Harrison Ltd. v. MacDonald & Evans [1952]: Under a contract of service, a man is employed as part of the business and his work is an integral part of the business; whereas under a contract for services, his work, although done for the business, is not integrated into it but is only accessory to it.
3. The Economic Reality / Multiple Test: Laid down in Ready Mixed Concrete (South East) Ltd. v. Minister of Pensions [1968]: Considers ownership of tools, provision of equipment, method of remuneration, power of dismissal, and commercial risk.

The crucial concept: "In the Course of Employment"
Sir John Salmond laid down the classic Salmond Test:
An act is within the course of employment if it is either:
(a) a wrongful act authorized by the master, or
(b) a wrongful and unauthorized mode of doing some act authorized by the master.
Key operational scenarios:
1. Careless or Negligent Performance: If an employee performs an authorized task carelessly, the master remains liable. In Century Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Northern Ireland Road Transport Board [1942], a petrol tanker driver struck a match to light a cigarette while transferring petrol into an underground tank, causing an explosion. The House of Lords held the master liable; lighting the cigarette was an unauthorized and negligent mode of conducting the authorized task of delivering petrol.
2. Express Prohibition by Master: An express prohibition against doing an act does not necessarily take it out of the course of employment. If the prohibited act was done to further the master’s business, the master is liable (Limpus v. London General Omnibus Co. [1862] — driver instructed not to race buses raced anyway to secure passengers; master liable). Conversely, if the prohibition limits the sphere of employment rather than the mode of conduct, the master is not liable (Twine v. Bean’s Express Ltd. — driver expressly forbidden from giving lifts; passenger injured was a trespasser to the employer).
3. Fraud and Wilful Wrongdoing: A master is liable for the fraud or theft committed by a servant in the course of employment, even if the fraud was committed entirely for the servant's personal enrichment (Lloyd v. Grace, Smith & Co. [1912] AC 716 — managing clerk of solicitors fraudulently induced client to convey property to him; solicitors held liable).
4. The "Frolic of His Own": Where a servant departs entirely from the master's business on a personal venture, the master is not liable (Joel v. Morrison (1834) — "a frolic of his own, without being at all on his master’s business").

State liability in India: The transition from sovereign immunity to constitutional torts
State liability in India is rooted in Article 300 of the Constitution, which links the liability of the Union of India or a State Government to that of the Dominion of India under the Government of India Act, 1858.

1. The Sovereign vs Non-Sovereign Fallacy (The Kasturi Lal Era):
   - In P. & O. Steam Navigation Co. v. Secretary of State for India (1861), Peacock, C.J. distinguished between acts done in exercise of "sovereign power" (no liability) and commercial/non-sovereign undertakings (liability attaches).
   - In Kasturi Lal Ralia Ram Jain v. State of U.P. (AIR 1965 SC 1039), police officers seized gold from a merchant under suspicion of theft. A police constable misappropriated the gold and fled to Pakistan. A Constitution Bench held that since the arrest and seizure were performed in exercise of sovereign statutory powers under the CrPC, the State was immune from civil liability. Chief Justice Gajendragadkar expressed regret at this unjust outcome and urged Parliament to enact legislation.

2. The Constitutional Revolution: Dismantling Sovereign Immunity via Public Law:
   Confronted with executive lawlessness, custodial deaths, and illegal detentions, the Supreme Court utilized Articles 32 and 226 to create the doctrine of Constitutional Torts, declaring sovereign immunity completely inapplicable to violations of Fundamental Rights under Article 21:
   - Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983) 4 SCC 141: Rudul Sah was detained in prison for 14 years after his judicial acquittal. The Supreme Court awarded monetary compensation of ₹35,000 under Article 32, establishing that compensation in public law is an acknowledged remedy for breach of Article 21.
   - Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993) 2 SCC 746: A 22-year-old youth died in police custody. The Supreme Court rejected the defence of sovereign immunity, holding that public law remedy for violation of human rights is distinct from private law tort actions and admits of no sovereign immunity defence.
   - D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) 1 SCC 416: Laid down mandatory arrest guidelines and held that custodial violence, torture, and custodial death strike at the rule of law, requiring state compensation.
   - N. Nagendra Rao & Co. v. State of A.P. (1994) 6 SCC 205: Held that in a modern welfare state, the demarcation between sovereign and non-sovereign functions has largely eroded. Sovereign immunity is restricted strictly to quintessential functions of the State (e.g. defence of the realm, foreign affairs, declaration of war). In all welfare, administrative, and regulatory actions, the State is vicariously answerable for the torts of its servants.

Procedural & forum anchors (Senior Counsel Reference)
- Competent Forum:
  1. Regular Civil Court: Suit against Master and Servant jointly and severally as joint tortfeasors.
  2. Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT): Suit against vehicle driver, registered owner (vicarious liability), and insurer.
  3. High Court (Art. 226) or Supreme Court (Art. 32): Writ petition for public law compensation against the State for custodial violence or arbitrary detention violating Article 21.
- Limitation Period:
  - Civil Court tort suit: Limitation Act 1963 Schedule Article 113 (3 years).
  - Special statutory protections: Pre-suit notice under Section 80 CPC (2 months mandatory notice before suing the Government or public officer).
- Evidentiary Burden:
  - Claimant must prove: (1) Tort committed by the employee, (2) Existence of employment contract, and (3) Close connection between wrongful act and the authorized course of duties.

Adversarial courtroom submissions
- Plaintiff / Victim Submissions:
  1. The wrongdoer was acting within the course of employment; the act was an unauthorized mode of an authorized task.
  2. The employer reaped the commercial benefit and is in control of the enterprise.
  3. In State actions: Sovereign immunity is constitutionally barred under Rudul Sah and Nilabati Behera where fundamental rights under Article 21 are violated.
- Defendant / Employer Submissions:
  1. The wrongdoer was an independent contractor, not an integrated employee.
  2. The employee was on a "frolic of his own," pursuing a private grudge or unauthorized personal enterprise.
  3. In State matters: Act falls within non-justiciable quintessential sovereign acts (defence, armed operations).

Current-law close
Under modern Indian law, the master is held strictly accountable for acts closely connected with employment, while the State’s archaic shield of sovereign immunity has been dismantled by the Supreme Court’s constitutional tort jurisprudence under Article 21.

examples.title: Example — course of employment (unauthorized mode)
examples.body: A bank cashier entrusted with accepting customer cash deposits takes ₹5 lakhs from a customer at the counter, issues a stamped bank receipt, but pockets the money and absconds. The bank contends that stealing money was never authorized. Held: Accepting deposits was an authorized duty; the theft was an unauthorized and fraudulent mode of performing that duty. The bank is vicariously liable to refund the customer with interest (Lloyd v. Grace, Smith & Co. and SBI v. Shyama Devi).

examples.title: Example — frolic of his own (employer not liable)
examples.body: A delivery driver employed by a departmental store completes his afternoon delivery route, parks the company delivery van at his residence, and later that evening takes the van without permission to drive forty miles to a distant nightclub with friends. On the way back at 2:00 AM, he negligently crashes into another car. Held: The driver was on a complete frolic of his own, outside the temporal and geographical scope of employment. The employer is not vicariously liable (Joel v. Morrison).

examples.title: Example — Constitutional Tort against the State
examples.body: An innocent young man is picked up by state police for questioning, subjected to third-degree custodial interrogation, and dies in police custody. The State pleads sovereign immunity on the ground that maintaining law and order is a sovereign function under Kasturi Lal. Held: Sovereign immunity cannot be pleaded against a claim under public law for infringement of the right to life under Article 21. The State is directed to pay ₹10 lakhs compensation to the deceased’s mother (Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa).

hypotheticals.question: Is the petrol pump owner vicariously liable for the assault committed by Dev? How will the court apply Salmond’s test and the doctrine of course of employment?
hypotheticals.analysis:
Under Salmond’s formulation, an employer is liable for an unauthorized act if it is an improper and wrongful mode of doing an authorized act. In Poland v. John Parr & Sons [1927], a carter struck a boy suspected of stealing sugar; the employer was held liable because the act was done in an over-zealous performance of an authorized duty.
Here, Dev was authorized to interact with customers, dispense fuel, and manage transactions at the forecourt. The dispute arose directly out of the service transaction (fuel meter reading). While the assault was unauthorized and contrary to company policy, it was intimately connected with the performance of his assigned duties. An express prohibition or criminal character does not automatically sever vicarious liability if the tort occurred within the general scope of customer service at the workplace.
Consequently, the assault was committed in the course of employment, making the employer vicariously liable as a joint tortfeasor.

misconceptions.trap: Assuming an employer escapes liability if the employee committed a deliberate crime or fraud.
misconceptions.correction: Under Lloyd v. Grace, Smith & Co., a master is liable for the fraud or crime of a servant if committed within the scope of apparent authority or course of employment, even if done solely for the servant’s private benefit.

misconceptions.trap: Believing sovereign immunity is still a valid defence against police brutality or custodial torture in India.
misconceptions.correction: The Supreme Court in Rudul Sah, Nilabati Behera, and D.K. Basu established that sovereign immunity is completely unavailable in public law proceedings under Article 32 and 226 for violations of Article 21.

cases.name: Lloyd v. Grace, Smith & Co.
cases.holding: A firm of solicitors was held vicariously liable for the fraud of their managing clerk who induced a client to transfer her property to him, even though the clerk acted entirely for his own benefit and without the knowledge of the partners.
cases.relevance: Established that a master is liable for the fraudulent acts of a servant committed in the course of employment.

cases.name: Century Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Northern Ireland Road Transport Board

questionsAndAnswers.question: Explain the doctrine of Vicarious Liability. When is a master held liable for the torts of his servant? Discuss with reference to the phrase "in the course of employment".
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
### 1. Introduction and Theoretical Foundation
Vicarious liability is an exception to the principle that a person is liable only for their own wrongful acts. In tort law, a master is held jointly and severally liable for the civil wrongs committed by their servant in the course of employment.
The doctrine is founded upon two Latin maxims:
1. Qui facit per alium facit per se: He who acts through another acts himself.
2. Respondeat Superior: Let the superior answer (the employer has a superior financial capacity and deep pocket).

### 2. Essential Ingredients
To establish vicarious liability, the plaintiff must prove:
1. The relationship of master and servant existed between the defendant and the tortfeasor.
2. The servant committed an actionable tort.
3. The tort was committed in the course of employment.

### 3. Meaning of "In the Course of Employment"
An act is done in the course of employment if it satisfies Salmond’s Test:
- It is either an authorized act, or
- An unauthorized, wrongful mode of doing an authorized act.

#### Key Principles:
1. Negligent Mode of Authorized Duty:
   In Century Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Northern Ireland Road Transport Board [1942] AC 509, a petrol tanker driver lit a cigarette while unloading petrol, triggering an explosion. The House of Lords held the master liable because delivering petrol was authorized; smoking was an unauthorized and careless mode of carrying out that authorized duty.
2. Fraud of Servant for Personal Gain:
   In Lloyd v. Grace, Smith & Co. [1912] AC 716, a solicitors' managing clerk fraudulently transferred a client’s cottages to himself. The House of Lords held the firm liable, ruling that a master is liable for a servant's fraud committed within apparent authority, even if solely for the servant's personal enrichment.
3. Express Prohibition:
   In Limpus v. London General Omnibus Co. (1862), a bus driver raced his vehicle contrary to express written orders not to obstruct rival buses. The master was held liable because the act was done in furtherance of the master’s business.
4. The Frolic of His Own (Exception):
   As laid down in Joel v. Morrison (1834), if a servant goes off on a "frolic of his own," pursuing purely personal ends without any connection to the master's business, the master is not liable.

### 4. Conclusion
Vicarious liability ensures that commercial enterprises internalize the risks of their operations and that injured citizens receive full compensatory recovery from the employer who created the enterprise and profited from the employee's labour.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Critically examine the liability of the State in tort in India. Trace the jurisprudential transition from the doctrine of Sovereign Immunity in Kasturi Lal to the modern regime of Constitutional Torts under Articles 21 and 32/226.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
### 1. Introduction and Constitutional Framework
The tortious liability of the State in India is governed by Article 300(1) of the Constitution of India, which provides that the Government of India or a State Government may sue or be sued in relation to their respective affairs in like cases as the Dominion of India might have sued or been sued under the Government of India Act, 1858. Because the 1858 Act codified the liability of the East India Company, Indian courts originally inherited archaic British doctrines of Crown immunity based on the maxim "The King can do no wrong" (Rex non potest peccare).

### 2. The Genesis of the Sovereign Immunity Dichotomy
#### A. P. & O. Steam Navigation Co. v. Secretary of State for India (1861)
Sir Barnes Peacock, C.J., in the Supreme Court of Calcutta, drew an artificial dividing line between:
1. Sovereign Functions: Acts done in exercise of sovereign power which could not be performed by a private individual (e.g. declaring war, making treaties). The State was immune.
2. Non-Sovereign Functions: Acts which could be performed by private commercial enterprises or individuals. The State was liable.

#### B. The Culmination of Crown Immunity: Kasturi Lal Ralia Ram Jain v. State of U.P. (AIR 1965 SC 1039)
In this case, police seized a large consignment of gold and silver from Kasturi Lal under suspicion of being stolen property. The gold was kept in police malkhana. A head constable misappropriated the gold and absconded to Pakistan. The merchant filed a suit for the return of gold or its value.
A Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court held:
1. The arrest of the merchant and seizure of property were performed by police officers in exercise of statutory powers under the Code of Criminal Procedure.
2. The power to arrest and seize property is a sovereign power delegated to police officers.
3. Consequently, the State was immune from vicarious liability, and the merchant was left without any civil remedy.
Although Chief Justice Gajendragadkar expressed grave concern and appealed to Parliament to pass legislation defining State liability, no statutory code was ever enacted.

### 3. The Judicial Revolution: Constitutional Torts and Article 21
Faced with police atrocities, custodial violence, and unlawful detention, the Supreme Court in the post-Emergency era bypassed the static common law of torts and forged the public law doctrine of Constitutional Torts under Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution.

#### A. Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983) 4 SCC 141
Rudul Sah was acquitted by a Sessions Court in 1968 but was illegally detained in prison for an additional 14 years until 1982. Chief Justice Y.V. Chandrachud awarded ₹35,000 as compensation under Article 32, declaring that Article 21 would be stripped of its significant content if the Court’s power was limited to merely releasing prisoners without providing compensatory restitution for state lawlessness.

#### B. Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993) 2 SCC 746
Suman Behera, a 22-year-old youth, was taken into police custody and found dead the next morning on a railway track with multiple blunt trauma injuries. The State pleaded sovereign immunity under Kasturi Lal.
The Supreme Court decisively rejected the plea:
- The Court established a clear distinction between private law tort claims and public law remedies under Articles 32 and 226.
- The defence of sovereign immunity is strictly confined to private law actions and is completely unavailable against violations of fundamental human rights under Article 21.
- Compensation was awarded to the mother of the deceased.

#### C. D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) 1 SCC 416
Justice A.S. Anand laid down comprehensive procedural guidelines for arrest and detention, holding that custodial violence is a direct attack on human dignity. Monetary compensation was declared to be an indispensable remedy in public law to penalize the state and heal the wounds of the victim.

### 4. Erosion of Sovereign Immunity in Statutory Actions
In N. Nagendra Rao & Co. v. State of A.P. (1994) 6 SCC 205, the State seized essential commodities (fertilizers) under the Essential Commodities Act, which spoiled due to negligent storage. The Supreme Court dismantled the sovereign function test:
"In the modern welfare state, where the state activities have expanded into commercial, industrial and social spheres, the concept of sovereign immunity has lost its relevance... Sovereign immunity is available only in strictly quintessential functions like defence, foreign affairs and declaring war."

### 5. Critical Analysis: The Contemporary Position
Today, Indian law operates on two distinct tiers:
1. In Public Law (Writs under Art. 32 and 226): Sovereign immunity is dead. Any violation of Article 21 by state actors (police brutality, illegal detention, encounters, custodial death) results in strict, immediate state compensation.
2. In Private Law (Regular Civil Suits): While Kasturi Lal has not been formally overruled by a larger bench, subsequent benches in Nagendra Rao and Common Cause v. Union of India have restricted sovereign immunity to an extreme vanishing point.

### 6. Conclusion
The transition from Kasturi Lal to Nilabati Behera reflects the transformation of Indian jurisprudence from colonial Crown immunity into constitutional accountability. In a republic governed by the Rule of Law and Article 21, the State cannot claim immunity for violating the fundamental rights of its citizens.

Basu under Art 21), and 3 marks for Nagendra Rao and modern synthesis.

revisionPoints: Maxims: Qui facit per alium facit per se & Respondeat Superior.
Three requirements: Master-servant relationship, commission of tort, and in the course of employment.
Course of Employment: Salmond’s test — authorized act or unauthorized mode of authorized act.
Century Insurance (1942): Negligently lighting match while unloading petrol was in course of employment.
Lloyd v. Grace, Smith (1912): Master is liable for fraud of servant committed within apparent authority.
State Liability: Article 300 Constitution of India.
Kasturi Lal (1965): Sovereign immunity upheld for police misappropriation of seized gold.
Constitutional Torts: Sovereign immunity abolished under Article 21 via Rudul Sah (1983) and Nilabati Behera (1993).
N. Nagendra Rao (1994): Sovereign immunity restricted to quintessential acts (defence, foreign affairs).
examTips: Always contrast Kasturi Lal with Nilabati Behera in chamber briefs and written submissions on State Liability.
Clearly distinguish between private law tort claims (where Kasturi Lal was decided) and public law constitutional remedies under Article 32/226.
Quote Salmond’s test for "course of employment" verbatim.
